title: NASA's Roman Space Telescope Launches on Mission to Map Dark Energy and Discover New Worlds
excerpt: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope lifted off aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy from Kennedy Space Center on Sunday, beginning a five-year mission to survey the cosmos with a field of view 100 times larger than Hubble's.
body:
• NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope lifted off aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy from Kennedy Space Center at 7:26 a.m. EDT on Sunday, Aug. 30.
  • The observatory will travel to a point one million miles from Earth and survey the cosmos with a field of view at least 100 times larger than Hubble's.
  • Its five-year primary mission will probe dark energy and dark matter, discover thousands of exoplanets, and study distant black holes.
  • ESA is contributing star trackers, batteries, and coronagraph detectors, and all science data will be publicly available with no proprietary period.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope lifted off aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from Launch Complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center in Florida at 7:26 a.m. EDT on Sunday, beginning what scientists expect will be a transformative mission in space observation.

Named after NASA's first chief astronomer, the observatory will travel to the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point, roughly one million miles from Earth, where it will begin scanning the cosmos in infrared light with resolution comparable to the Hubble Space Telescope — but a field of view at least 100 times wider.

A Panoramic Eye on the Cosmos

Roman carries two primary instruments: a 300-megapixel Wide Field Instrument capable of crisp visible and near-infrared imaging, and a coronagraph designed to block starlight and directly image faint planets orbiting distant stars. The telescope's 2.4-meter primary mirror — originally built for another government agency and adapted for NASA's needs — will collect and focus light from cosmic objects near and far.

https://x.com/NASA/status/2094017464216563968

By the end of its five-year primary mission, with NASA targeting a full 10-year operational life, Roman is expected to generate a 20,000-terabyte data archive. Scientists plan to use it to identify and study 100,000 exoplanets, hundreds of millions of galaxies, and billions of stars.

"Roman's accelerated development is a true success story of what we can achieve when public investment, institutional expertise, and private enterprise come together to take on the near-impossible missions that change the world."

— Jared Isaacman, NASA Administrator

Probing the Dark Universe

About 95% of the universe is composed of dark energy and dark matter, both invisible to conventional observation. Roman will tackle both mysteries using multiple methods.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=h_p4pc2DmKY

One of its core surveys will scan roughly 12% of the sky for weak gravitational lensing — the subtle warping of distant galaxy shapes caused by intervening dark matter. By mapping these distortions across cosmic history, astronomers will trace how matter clumped together over billions of years.

To study the mysterious force driving the universe's accelerating expansion, Roman will hunt for Type Ia supernovae in distant galaxies, using their predictable brightness as cosmic distance markers. It will also map baryonic acoustic oscillations — ripple patterns frozen into the distribution of galaxies since the early universe — to measure how expansion has changed over time.

Hunting Exoplanets and Extreme Events

Roman's deep, wide surveys of the Milky Way's center are expected to reveal more than 1,200 new worlds through gravitational microlensing and over 100,000 transiting planets. The coronagraph will attempt to directly image exoplanets by suppressing starlight by a factor of more than 100 million.

The telescope is also sensitive enough to detect extreme cosmic events, including tidal disruption events where supermassive black holes shred passing stars, dating back 11 billion years. Recent research published in The Astrophysical Journal suggests Roman could be "transformative for transient science," according to lead author Mitchell Karmen of Johns Hopkins University.

International Collaboration, Open Data

While NASA-led, the mission draws on significant international contributions. The European Space Agency is providing star trackers, batteries, coronagraph detectors, and communications support through its deep-space ground station network, including a new 35-meter antenna in New Norcia, Australia.

"Whenever astronomy opens a new window on the Universe, history has shown that some of the most important discoveries are the ones we never anticipated."

— Bethan James, ESA's Roman Project Scientist

All science data will be publicly available with no proprietary period, and a substantial fraction of observing time will be reserved for community-proposed research beyond the core surveys. The mission is managed at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, with participation from the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Caltech/IPAC, and the Space Telescope Science Institute. Primary industrial partners include Ball Aerospace, L3Harris Technologies, and Teledyne Scientific & Imaging.
